In this garden, the Collection pattern models a curated collection whose members are all instances of some other entity type. It is not instantiated directly — it is specialized per member type as <EntityType>/Collection (e.g. Logseq/Entity/Software/Plugin/Collection), and each specialization points back here for the shared rules.
The pattern, and the reserved /Collection segment

A specialization lives at the member type's namespace with a trailing /Collection segment. That trailing segment is a reserved pattern marker: X/Collection means "a curated collection whose members are instances of X" (a collection-of-X), not a kind-of-X. This deliberately reverses how namespace nesting usually reads — Software/Plugin is a plugin, but Software/Plugin/Collection is a collection of plugins. The flip applies only to the reserved trailing /Collection segment.
The pattern, and the reserved /Collection segment

This is a different axis from Logseq/Entity → multiple entity membership. Multiple membership = one page is several entity types at once (e.g. Question + Card). The Collection pattern = one page is a single entity whose members are of type X. (A collection page may still use multiple membership for unrelated reasons.)
Common shape — what every collection shares
Curated — an intentional, purposeful selection, not an arbitrary or exhaustive list.
Common shape — what every collection shares
Typed members — members are instances of one declared entity type (the X in X/Collection).
Common shape — what every collection shares
Has identity — the collection is itself an entity with its own page, name, and purpose/curator.
Common shape — what every collection shares
Ordered or unordered — each specialization states which (a series is ordered; a pack is unordered).
Common shape — what every collection shares
Logseq/Entity/Software/Plugin/Collection — curated collections of plugins for a host (LazyVim extras, VS Code Extension Packs, …).
Ordered sequences of another entity type are Logseq/Entity/Series, not a Collection specialization.
When to create a new specialization

Lazily. Create X/Collection only when there is a real instance to file under it — the pattern earns generality from use, not speculation. Candidates that may earn pages later: Book/Collection (a series/anthology), Article/Collection (a special issue), a playlist, a card deck.
When to create a new specialization

Instances declare the specialization, not this pattern page: e.g. logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Software/Plugin/Collection]]. This page is the shared definition each specialization references.
Mirrors established collection primitives: skos:Collection, bibo:Collection / bibo:Series, and parametric container types (Collection<T>).

In this garden, Color Theme pages model coordinated palette families (foreground, background, accent colors) reused across terminals, editors, multiplexers, file managers, and other UI tools. A color-theme instance is the aesthetic system (e.g. Catppuccin with subpages Catppuccin/Latte, Catppuccin/Frappe, Catppuccin/Macchiato, Catppuccin/Mocha); individual ports often stay Logseq/Entity/Software/Project instance pages that link back to the theme hub.
Catppuccin — hub with palette overview asset, stack matrix, and flavor subpages for per-variant config ids and previews.
When we treat something as a color theme

Strong signals: a named palette family with official style-guide or palette specs; many first- or third-party ports sharing the same flavor names; users think in terms of “using X everywhere” (terminal, editor, shell tools).
When we treat something as a color theme
Weak signals alone (a single app’s built-in scheme with no shared branding) are usually not a color-theme entity — note them on the app page instead.
When we treat something as a color theme
How to name the main page for a color theme
Prefer a short top-level name when the theme name is unambiguous (e.g. Catppuccin), matching the spirit of software project hubs like Lazygit.
How to name the main page for a color theme

A hierarchical path under a UI namespace goes in alias:: only when codekiln asks for it, such as alias:: [[UI/Color/Theme/Catppuccin]] on the Catppuccin page for visibility under , per My/AI/Rule/Logseq/No Aliases Unless Asked.
How to name the main page for a color theme

Use Theme/Flavor sub-namespaces when the upstream theme names discrete variants (e.g. Catppuccin’s four flavors): hub page links the set; each subpage holds typical config keywords, optional preview image from ../assets/…, and points back to the hub for the full stack matrix. For themes without named variants, keep a single hub section instead.
How to name the main page for a color theme

Check in this order: exact page name, exact alias, official homepage or org/repo, then page-body mentions of the same palette names and upstream links. Classify as: existing, similar, new, or blocked.

Official or community ports (Neovim plugin repo, tmux plugin, etc.) can be software project entities with logseq-entity:: Logseq/Entity/Software/Project; they should link to the color-theme hub for palette and flavor semantics. The theme hub lists app wiring without duplicating full plugin documentation.
To mark a page as a color-theme instance, add logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Color/Theme]] in frontmatter. The type page then gets backlinks to all color-theme pages.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
File: pages/<ThemeName>.md for the short name. First block: H1 with a link to the official site or palette repo.

Keep a lean hub: identity, flavor index (links to Theme/Flavor subpages or inline list if no subpages), optional overview image in assets/ with source footnote, palette reference (link out), stack matrix (per app: mechanism, config hook, links to Ghostty, nvim, tmux, yazi, etc., and to config subpages when detail lives there). Put per-flavor detail (ids, previews) on subpages when they exist.

In this garden, Company pages model commercial vendors, businesses, product firms, devtool vendors, consulting companies, and brands tracked as first-class pages—often because they ship multiple Logseq/Entity/Software/Project pages linked with created-by::.
Charm — vendor behind the Charmbracelet GitHub org; created-by:: [[Charm]] on gum; ecosystem siblings include glow and Glamour.
Jellyfish — engineering management platform (Boston); is co-founder and CEO; appears on iia/1130 Built in Boston Scaling Global AI Company.
When we treat something as a company
Strong signals: official site positioning as a company or team, a stable trade name, GitHub org or product suite under one brand, or notes that keep returning to “who makes this.”
When we treat something as a company

Not a company entity: non-company standards bodies, foundations, nonprofits, public institutions, consortia, professional associations, or governance/community bodies. Use Logseq/Entity/Organization for those.
When we treat something as a company
Prefer a person entity when the subject is an individual maintainer; use company when the subject is the organization or brand (even if it is small).
When we treat something as a company
How to name the main page for a company
Prefer a short top-level name that matches natural garden linking, such as Charm for “Charm” even when the GitHub org is charmbracelet.
How to name the main page for a company
Alternate names (legal name, GitHub org label, “Foo Inc.” vs “Foo”) go in alias:: only when codekiln asks for them, per My/AI/Rule/Logseq/No Aliases Unless Asked.
How to name the main page for a company
If the company is only context for one product and unlikely to recur, the vendor can be documented inline on the software page. Create a company entity when the organization is likely to recur.
How to name the main page for a company
Check in this order: exact page name, exact alias, official domain, GitHub org name, then page-body mentions of the same site or org. Classify as: existing, similar, new, or blocked.

Software entities may set created-by:: [[CompanyName]] when the maintainer is the organization and a company page exists. If the creator is an individual with a page, use that instead (or both only when both are accurate and useful).
To mark a page as a company instance, add logseq-entity:: with a link to this type page in frontmatter. The type page then gets backlinks to all company pages.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
File: pages/<CompanyName>.md for the short name. First block: H1 with a link to the official site (or primary public presence).
Keep the page lean: what the company is, notable products or org links, and backlinks from software entities.

In this garden, Concept pages model understanding-oriented topics that follow the garden’s Diataxis-style shape (aligned with Diataxis/Concept / Diataxis/Explanation): paradigms, architectural lenses, and other “big ideas” explained rather than only defined.
When we treat something as a concept entity
Strong signals: the page’s purpose is understanding—what something is, why it matters, how it relates to neighboring ideas—not primarily a how-to, tutorial walkthrough, or lookup reference.
When we treat something as a concept entity
Good fit: programming paradigms, frameworks of thought, architectural patterns explained in prose.
When we treat something as a concept entity

Link shape: [[Topic/Concept/Idea]] or [[Topic/Explanation/Idea]] when the topic has enough pages to want the segment, as on Programming/Language/Concept/Object-Oriented and herdr/Explanation/Where Input Box Text Comes From.
A concept that is the topic takes the topic's own name, as cybernetics does.
Search for an existing page before creating a new concept entity.
Search order hints: exact title, alternate titles from frontmatter, normalized topic phrases, sibling pages in the same topic area.
Classify as: existing, similar (needs human judgment), new, or blocked.
On instances, set logseq-entity:: to a link to this entity-type page so backlinks list all concept entities.
Concept-specific tags may mirror the established Diataxis concept cluster when the page is new and that convention applies.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Use Logseq Flavored Markdown (bullets, headings as bullets, tab nesting, no blank lines between bullets).
Recommended sections (Diataxis explanation style): Overview, Context, Key Principles, Mechanism, Examples, Misconceptions. Adapt headings to the topic; not every section must be long.
First heading after frontmatter: H1 matching the page’s primary topic.
Concept stays first in logseq-entity::, and the other type follows it.

In this garden, Course pages model a named course of study with a coherent purpose, teaching team, and learning activities.
The course page holds the identity and educational purpose shared across offerings. A dated teaching plan is a Logseq/Entity/Course/Syllabus instance linked from the course.
A book, a single talk, and a collection of unrelated resources each retain their own entity definitions.
A course with an established provider or creator namespace follows Logseq/Pref/Page/Name under that namespace with a Course segment. Otherwise its title is Course/<Course Name>.

Search the official URL, full course title, shorter public name, instructor, and provider before creating a course. A new term or syllabus revision belongs to the existing course when the course's identity continues.
logseq-entity:: points to this definition. Shared conventions follow Logseq/Frontmatter.
instructor:: links the teaching staff's Logseq/Entity/Person hubs, including professor instances where applicable. created-by:: credits course designers when the source identifies them.
provider:: links an existing institution or organization page when the source establishes that relationship; otherwise the provider can be stated in prose.
A linked H1 points to the official course site and uses its public course name.
About describes the subject, audience, learning aims, and approach.
Offering records the term, format, location, participation conditions, and fee when published, with dates attributed to the relevant offering.
Syllabus links the dated syllabus pages. Detailed assignments and meeting schedules live on those pages.
Source disagreements are stated beside the affected fact, with enough context to identify each source.
In this garden, Course Syllabus pages model a dated plan for one offering of a course, including its aims, expectations, schedule, and assigned material.
A syllabus belongs to a Logseq/Entity/Course instance. Its title is <Course Page>/Syllabus/<Year Term>; distinct published revisions may append a source revision label.
A syllabus page carries this entity alone in logseq-entity::; it describes a course document, while the parent course page describes the course itself.

Compare course identity, academic term, source URL, and stated revision before creating another syllabus. Revisions for the same offering can update one page when the source and revision history remain clear.
course:: links the course instance. academic-term:: records the source's year and term. syllabus-status:: records a published status such as Draft or Final when stated.
created-by:: credits the syllabus author when identified. A source filename or upload directory alone does not establish its publication date.
A linked H1 points to the original syllabus and names the course and offering.
Overview summarizes the learning aims and teaching approach in original prose, with the document's draft status and source revision when available.
Requirements preserves attendance, written work, group activities, personal practice, participation conditions, and support information.
Required books links the Logseq/Entity/Book instances explicitly required for purchase or sustained use.

Schedule has one dated heading per meeting, with required and recommended assignments kept distinct. Assignments preserve chapter titles, page ranges, case identifiers, media formats, alternatives, and details still awaiting confirmation.
Assigned books link to their book pages; named authors, speakers, and case subjects link to their person hubs. Chapters remain assignment text unless they have substantive section pages of their own.
An adaptation credits its remote source and summarizes explanatory prose. Unspecified readings and provisional sessions retain their uncertainty.

entity-tasks:: declares the Logseq/Entity/Mise/Task reference pages needed to work with instances of this entity. The property is a comma-separated list of wikilinks in the definition's frontmatter; an absent property declares no companion tasks.

Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page/mise/Task/sync follows an instance's logseq-entity:: links, imports its entity definitions, and follows each definition's entity-tasks:: links. Task references declare their executable files and required task dependencies through the companion-file contract on Logseq/Entity/Mise/Task.
Shared entity definitions and task dependencies are visited once per sync. Cyclic relationships are allowed and terminate after their pages have been visited.

A referenced entity definition with no source file is reported as a logical page. A declared companion task or task dependency requires a source reference page and its mapped implementation files; missing task content stops application.

entity-proxy-destination-properties:: names, as a comma-separated list of property keys, the properties on an instance that belong to the garden holding a Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page of it rather than to the source page. Re-syncing that proxy keeps the destination's values for them. An absent property names none.
For example, Logseq/Entity/Podcast/Episode names podcast-guid and podcast-published-at, which the publishing garden records.

Logseq/Entity is the general conceptual model — what an entity is and how any page is marked as one. This page is the entity type whose instances are the definition pages themselves, so the garden's set of entity types is queryable through its backlinks rather than kept as a hand-maintained list.
The Entities System - Conceptual Overview and Vision
The Entities System - Conceptual Overview and Vision

My/Entity/System is an approach to Knowledge Gardens where a distinct, identified part of the garden defines the kinds of entities in that garden. While it was originally adopted within Logseq using Logseq/Namespaces, it has also been adopted in Obsidian using folders. The disucssion here uses examples from Logseq, but the principles of the Entities System are intended to be independent of the technology used for knowledge gardening. The basic idea is that you have your entity definitions in one place, separated from the rest of the pages that "take on" one or more entity definitions so as to signify the "is-a" relationship.

The Entities System is a form of a collection or curation of Design/Patterns, just applied to Knowledge Gardening.

The evolution of a knowledge garden and its kinds of entities are alive in the sense that Person/Christopher Alexander/Book/77/A Pattern Language describes a system of Design/Patterns. Quoting that book:

The Entities System is Similar to Diagram/Entity Relationship for a particular domain of inquiry or field of study. An Entity Relationship Diagram or ERD is a tool, a perspective for how to think about a system. It's key to keep in mind that it's a perspective, and as such, it's incomplete. Just as Person/Christopher Alexander talks about how each Design/Pattern is a hypothesis, the entities in a knowledge garden are first or second order approximations of the in human Conscious/ness. They must always be considered to be lossy representations.
The Entities System - Conceptual Overview and Vision

The Entities System is influenced by the concept of DDL in Database/System/Theory. One can think of the entity definitions as comparable to the Schema for the database: the code which declares the tables and the types of the columns in a database.

In alignment with My/Principle/Declarative over Imperative, I would prefer for the Entities System to converge on Declarative definitions rather than Imperative ones. It may take some time to achieve on that goal, so I ask for your help and patience in this asymptotic effort. What would this mean? It would mean that each page is less a set of instructions of how to do things, and more a description of what the page is, leaving the "how" to an externally intelligent entity such as a human or an AI/Agent to bring its creativity to bare on how to meet the spirit of the definition.

In this garden, Diataxis pages model documentation written for one reader need from the Diataxis framework: doing a task, learning a skill, looking something up, or understanding why.
Each child entity below extends this one. Pick the child by what the reader needs.
A page that serves one of the four needs. A topic that needs two of them gets two pages, each linking to the other.
Each child definition page says what its own instances look like and which of its siblings a near miss belongs to.
An instance carries its child entity alone: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/How To]]. The child already says the page is a Diataxis page.
When the page is also another entity, that entity comes first and the Diataxis child follows it: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/CLI/Command]], [[Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/How To]].
tags:: — a new page carries its child's tag from the table above, alongside its topic tags.
see-also:: — preferred over a ## Related section that only lists internal wikilinks.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Each child entity defines its own namespace, page shape and voice.
A page links out to its siblings when the reader needs them, so a how-to links to the explanation behind a step and leaves the explaining to that page.

In this garden, Diataxis Explanation pages model understanding-oriented writing: why something is the way it is, and how ideas fit together. They explain why and serve understanding, the reflective quadrant of Diataxis.
Choosing between the four children, marking an instance, see-also:: and shared frontmatter follow Logseq/Entity/Diataxis.
A page that gives background, weighs alternatives, or draws the connections between ideas, rather than instructing or cataloguing.
Not an instance: a page of steps — Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/How To or Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/Tutorial. A systematic description of a thing — Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/Reference.

This quadrant overlaps the entity system almost entirely: an explanation-shaped page in this garden is normally a concept instance, and Logseq/Entity/Concept governs its frontmatter, its naming, and its body sections.

Read Logseq/Entity/Concept first, then this page for the Diataxis vocabulary and the tag. Where the two differ, the Concept page wins on shape and this page wins on which quadrant the writing belongs to.
Logseq/Entity/Term covers the narrower case of naming a thing rather than explaining it; a page can be both.
No namespace segment of its own — an explanation page is named for the idea it explains, wherever that idea naturally sits, per Logseq/Entity/Concept.
tags:: — new pages of this kind carry [[Diataxis/Concept]] (or [[Diataxis/Explanation]], the same cluster by alias).
Per Logseq/Entity/Concept. This entity adds no shape of its own.
Take a wider view than a task allows: the history, the alternatives that were not taken, the reasons behind a design.
Admit the disagreements. Explanation is the one quadrant where opinion belongs, provided it is marked as such.
Link out to the how-to, tutorial and reference pages rather than absorbing their jobs.
Diataxis/Explanation — the framework concept page this entity implements.

Logseq/Entity/Discussion — a Discussion page that weighs alternatives also carries this entity, after Discussion in its logseq-entity:: line. It takes its name, placement, shape and frontmatter from the Discussion definition, so an agent writing one leaves out the [[Diataxis/Concept]] tag that new Explanation pages otherwise carry.

In this garden, Diataxis How To pages model goal-oriented directions that walk a competent reader through solving one specific problem. They inform action and serve the application of a skill, the practical quadrant of Diataxis.
Choosing between the four children, marking an instance, see-also:: and shared frontmatter follow Logseq/Entity/Diataxis.
A page addressing a real-world task the reader already knows they want to accomplish, written as a sequence of steps rather than as teaching or description.

Not an instance: a page that teaches a skill the reader does not yet have — that is Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/Tutorial. A page that describes what something is — that is Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/Reference. A page that explains why — that is Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/Explanation.
